effect_estimate.comment: Synthesizes baseline survey market shares, cluster-randomized revealed-preference logistic regression models (Models 1-5), demand forecasts, stated-preference multinomial logit WTP estimates (Model 9), and operational/overhead cost-subsidy gap models. Note that the Abstract cites US$44 production cost and US$20 subsidy at US$24 price (corresponding to rounded opex/partial cost figures), whereas Table 8 and Section 4 report US$61 total cost per empty at 4 pits/day with an owned exhauster truck (US$32 opex + US$29 overhead), requiring a US$37/empty subsidy (US$0.36/month surcharge).
effect_estimate.value: In revealed-preference logistic regressions of Pit Vidura formal pit-emptying requests over 90 days following village-level coupon price randomization, higher individual price per 1,200 L empty (US$) significantly reduced uptake across all models (Model 1, Any Empty, N = 1,176: log-odds beta = -0.036, SE = 0.008, p < 0.01; Model 2, Group Empty, N = 1,176: beta = -0.036, SE = 0.011, p < 0.01; Model 3, N = 1,078: beta = -0.035, SE = 0.008, p < 0.01; Model 4, N = 1,156: beta = -0.038, SE = 0.009, p < 0.01; Model 5, N = 1,065: beta = -0.041, SE = 0.014, p < 0.01). Neighbor group-empty price discounts (US$) increased requests in Model 2 (Group Empty: beta = 0.103, SE = 0.056, p < 0.1) and Model 3 (Any Empty: beta = 0.084, SE = 0.041, p < 0.05), becoming non-significant after controlling for pit fullness (Model 4: beta = 0.070, SE = 0.044; Model 5: beta = 0.067, SE = 0.066). Household (vs. sole landlord) responsibility for pit maintenance costs increased service requests in Model 3 (beta = 0.714, SE = 0.328, p < 0.05; 64% +/- 2.9% of households responsible at baseline, N = 1,078). Model 1 3-month demand forecasts were 0.4% (95% CI: 0.03-4%) at US$115.8, 1.5% or ~15% of full pits (95% CI: 0.21-9%) at US$79.0, 5.0% or half of full pits (95% CI: 1.28-17%) at US$44.8, and 10.0% or all full pits (95% CI: 3.69-24%) at US$24.2 (compared with 0.42% baseline 3-month formal emptying coverage). In the stated-preference multinomial logit model (Model 9, N = 157; price beta = -0.013, p < 0.01), households had significant WTP premiums (US$/empty above informal manual emptying) for pit sealing (US$152, p < 0.01), sludge treatment (US$136, p < 0.01), distant disposal (US$89.7, p < 0.01), and branded formal service with worker protections (US$84.3, p < 0.01), preferred volumetric pricing over flat fees (flat fee WTP = -US$48.1, p < 0.01), and were indifferent to faster response (1 vs. 3 weeks: US$16.2, NS) and emptying only when full (US$5.62, NS). Full service cost ranged from US$61/empty (owned 10 m3 exhauster truck at 4 pits/day) to US$191/empty (rented 5 m3 flatbed truck at 1 pit/day); achieving universal emptying at US$24/empty against US$61/empty cost requires a US$37/empty subsidy (coverable via a US$0.36/month surcharge on the existing US$2/month municipal solid waste fee; Abstract also cites US$44 production cost and US$20 subsidy).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Coupon volumetric prices and group-coordination discounts (fees/subsidies) were cluster-randomized across 30 villages and linked to observed service requests over 90 days (experimental evidence under RoB 2 cluster-randomized trial appraisal). Caveats include household-level logit estimation without explicit cluster-adjusted standard errors, missing group-vs-individual breakdown for 14 unserved requesters, observational estimation for landlord vs. household maintenance responsibility, and stated-preference estimation for response speed and service formalization.

sample_size.comment: At baseline (Survey 1), 1,167 households across 30 villages received coupons; 62 households requested Pit Vidura services (including 12 non-coupon neighbor households in group empties, making N = 1,179, of which 3 neighbor households lacking coupon numbers were dropped, leaving N = 1,176 in Models 1-2, N = 1,078 in Model 3, N = 1,156 in Model 4, and N = 1,065 in Model 5). Follow-up Surveys 2 and 3 (including the stated-preference discrete choice experiment) covered 157 households/landlords (50 service requesters plus 107 non-requesters). Sub-analyses in Table 6 and Figure 1 had item-specific N ranging from 15 to 1,156.

study_design.comment: Combines (1) a cluster-randomized revealed-preference field experiment assigning 12 volumetric price and group-discount coupon versions across 30 villages (analyzed via household-level logistic regression), (2) a follow-up stated-preference discrete choice experiment with randomized choice sets (analyzed via multinomial logit), and (3) activity-based operational and overhead cost modeling of rented flatbed vs. owned exhauster truck scenarios from Pit Vidura expense reports.
study_design.value: Cluster-randomized revealed-preference price-coupon trial across 30 villages (with logistic regression demand modeling), combined with a follow-up stated-preference discrete choice survey (multinomial logit) and operational/overhead service-cost gap analysis
